title: Dungeons on Automatic monster descriptions for the Enraged Eggplant package
summary: Original DOA-authored reader-facing prose. The authorized fan-conversion source is a GURPS mechanics conversion and states no creature descriptions, so there is nothing to import and nothing withheld; these are written from each record's own converted statistics and from this project's art direction for the creature. No SRD text is a permitted basis: SRD 3.5 prose is OGL 1.0a and cannot be carried into a CC BY field. See review/policy/description-policy.md.

descriptions.text: A hulking amphibious predator of lightless underground water, heavy through the body and smooth as an eel, with three stacked eyes and four long tentacles that it drags itself along on when it leaves the shallows. It thinks in inherited memory older than most civilisations, speaks mind to mind, and regards the surface and everyone on it as livestock.

A flightless bird the size of a warhorse, walking on four stiff obsidian legs with a compact armoured body slung between them. It keeps to burnt, sulfur-smelling country where organised cruelty is ordinary, kills with a hooked beak and heavy claws, and takes its time about it.

What is left of someone who died insane: a tattered upper body trailing away into smoke, no legs beneath it, hands drawn out too long. It cannot form words, only a rising babble that scatters thought, and its touch leaves the living hallucinating. Religious symbols drive it back.

A six-legged burrowing arthropod as heavy as a pony, with shovel-like foreclaws and mandibles that run with digestive acid. Nearly blind and completely deaf, it hunts by the tremor of footsteps overhead, erupting out of tilled soil to seize whatever is passing and drag it under.

A spider the size of a large dog, dun-coloured and hunched, with a swollen hump on its back that holds a brain as capable as a person's. It spins, it bites, and it can rearrange what a victim believes they are seeing. Fire is the one thing that reliably breaks its nerve.

A feathered, legless hunter of the open air, built like a barbed dart with a hooked beak at the front and a rudder of a tail behind. It never lands willingly, spits arcs of lightning at range, and treats anything sharing its sky as an intruder to be driven off.

A sphere of steady white-gold light no bigger than a helm, with no body to speak of: no face, no limbs, nothing an ordinary weapon can find. It drifts rather than walks, answers questions honestly and at some length, and fights fiends with lances of focused light while refusing to harm anyone innocent.

A tall dog-headed warrior in plain gold-chased steel, carrying a greatsword in both hands. It smells a lie the way it smells a trail, sees through invisibility without effort, and hunts fiends with patient discipline — but will not raise the blade against anyone innocent, whatever the cost.

A tall winged warrior in restrained silver-and-brass plate, a greatsword at the ready and a brass trumpet slung at the hip. The horn is not ceremonial: its note carries orders across a battlefield and staggers anything unholy that hears it. Honest to a fault, and unwilling to strike the innocent.

A thick braided creeper with muscular tendrils, black recurved thorns and pale bell-shaped flowers, lying among ordinary undergrowth it cannot be told apart from. Blind and deaf, it waits for weight and warmth to pass within reach, then wraps and squeezes until whatever it caught stops moving and rots into the soil beneath it.

A tall winged figure with luminous skin and broad silver-white feathers, armoured in pearl-grey steel under an indigo mantle and carrying a heavy ceremonial mace. Beautiful in a way that is difficult to look at directly, it will not lie, and it knows an unholy thing the moment one enters the room.

A short, heavily built humanoid with ember-dark skin and a crest of living flame where hair would be, at home in forge heat and worked copper. Fire does not trouble it in the slightest; cold cuts twice as deep. It fights with a two-handed warhammer built for its own broad frame.

A hulking, badly assembled giant with mottled stone-grey hide, a lopsided tusked mouth, and a third arm growing from its chest that it uses as readily as the other two. It can be smelled well before it is seen, swings a knotted club the size of a young tree, and its bite carries a venom that leaves victims weakening for hours.

An ordinary brown rat, quick and low to the ground, with a bare tail as long as its body and small blunt claws. Alone it is barely a threat to anyone armed; in a granary, a bilge or a sewer it is never alone, and it will bite a sleeper without hesitation.

A rat grown to the size of a large dog, heavy through the shoulders, with coarse charcoal fur, torn ears and incisors that shear through boot leather. It moves almost silently along drains and flooded cellars, and unlike its smaller kin it is bold enough to go for a standing adult.

A human-shaped absence rather than a figure: layered translucent black, hands drawn out too long, no legs at all, drifting a few inches clear of the floor. Its touch draws the strength out of a body by degrees, ordinary blows pass through it, and direct sunlight burns it away.

A powerfully built winged figure with bronze-olive skin and broad ivory feathers, armoured in pearl-grey steel and carrying an oversized greatsword in both hands. Wounds close on it while you watch. It is patient, entirely truthful, and quite certain of what it has been sent to do.

The most commanding of the winged host: deep umber skin, silver-black hair, vast white-and-gold wings, a dark blue and electrum cuirass, a greatsword across the back and a recurved longbow already in hand. Its voice alone carries authority. Very little that opposes it survives the first exchange.

A burrowing worm of articulated black volcanic stone, its segment joints split by seams of orange-white magma. It has no mouth and no interest in eating; it tunnels through rock by melting a path, and anything it slams into or simply touches is scorched by the heat coming off it.

A wiry blue-scaled humanoid about four feet tall, with webbed hands and feet, external gill frills and a pair of translucent fin-wings that shed water constantly. It is curious, mouthy and fond of a bad joke, and it spits a hard jet of water that knocks a person off their feet more often than it hurts them.

A small, wiry ash-grey creature with a hunched spine, oversized ears, a thin tail and long black claws. It is a liar and a nuisance by nature, takes another shape when hiding suits it better, and enjoys the trouble it causes considerably more than any fight it picks.

A muscular dragon scaled in pearl-white and pale blue, with a low wedge of a head, backward-swept horns like ice crystal and a long spined tail. It swims and climbs as readily as it flies, breathes a killing cold, and is the least clever and most direct of its kind about what it wants and how it intends to take it.

A low, heavy lizard about as long as a man is tall, running on eight short legs, rough-scaled in olive and ochre with a blunt wedge of a head. It is slow, ill-tempered and entirely unhurried, because it has no need of speed: whatever meets its glowing amber eyes stops being flesh.

A heavier, meaner basilisk, running on eight legs under layered charcoal and bruised-purple scales with iron-hard spines along its back and a barbed tail behind. Four ember-red eyes sit in one broad head, and meeting them is as fatal as meeting the smaller kind's two. Magic slides off it.

An unnaturally thin biped whose oil-slick black skin sheds light, with a bone-plated skull of a face, a wide predatory mouth and long clawed fingers. It moves in complete silence, prefers ambush to confrontation, and takes its time once the outcome is no longer in doubt.

A hulking assembly of mismatched corpses, grey and bruised-brown, held together by dark sutures and heavy iron staples, with a copper conductor cage across the shoulders. It is silent, mindless and does exactly what it is told. Spells break against it uselessly, and when it is hurt badly enough it stops taking orders at all.

A barrel of mottled hide standing on three splayed legs, with a tooth-lined maw opening in the front of its body, small eyes clustered above it, and two long tentacle-arms ending in rough gripping pads. It lives in filth by preference, eats anything, and can be smelled long before the corridor turns.

A crude, heavy-shouldered giant roughly twice the height of a man, weather-darkened and dressed in patched hides. It lives by taking — herds, carts, travellers — throws boulders at whatever it cannot reach on foot, and settles the rest with a round-headed maul of wood and stone.

A gaunt corpse eight feet tall, charcoal-grey and desiccated, its narrow skull eyeless and its chest opened into a hollow cage of asymmetrical ribs. What it wants is what fills that cavity. It is patient about getting it, and neither poison, terror nor persuasion has any purchase on it.

A lean, scarred figure in an iron half-mask, wearing a mantle of interlocked black chain that does not hang the way metal should. The chains move at its will, striking from angles no arm could reach, and it holds a victim's gaze while they do. It heals what you cut, and it is in no hurry.

A heavy, low-slung quadruped in soot-black fur striped with iron grey, with a broad hyena-like muzzle, ember eyes and oversized claws. It hunts thinking prey deliberately and for preference, and what it consumes is beyond the reach of any resurrection.

A serpentine bulk a dozen yards long in cobalt and bronze scale, running on twelve hooked legs that let it climb a cavern wall as easily as cross its floor. It can shed the legs and coil instead, crushing what it has wrapped, and it spits a bolt of lightning down a corridor when coiling is too slow.

A wiry rust-red creature the size of a cat, with small leathery wings, swept-back brow horns and a thin tail ending in a sting. It prefers another shape in company, whispers bad advice with real fluency, and is far harder to be rid of than its size suggests.

A soot-black thing of living smoke with a narrow predatory head, white-hot eyes and two long clawed arms, its lower body trailing off into a spiralling column. It can thin into ordinary smoke to pass a doorway or a grille, and it prefers to attack from inside a fire's own haze.

A stocky crimson-brown soldier in piecemeal black iron, square-horned, barb-tailed, carrying a glaive. The beard is a mass of short quill-like tendrils and it moves on its own, striking at anyone who closes. It fights with more enthusiasm than judgement and does not stop when it should.

A lean golden-tan hound with a dark muzzle, bright blue-white eyes and travel-worn paws, no larger than a big working dog. It fights by vanishing and reappearing at the edge of reach, so a swing meant for it lands where it was. It keeps company with its own kind and dislikes evil things on principle.

A gaunt charcoal-grey figure, hairless, lipless, with dim corpse-white eyes recessed under a smooth skull. It was a person once and remembers it in fragments. Meeting its stare is lethal on its own, and whatever it kills that way has a habit of standing up later in the same condition.

An armoured burrowing predator several yards long, with a blue-black dorsal shell, a pale shovel-shaped head and a maw that closes on stone as readily as on meat. It tracks prey by vibration through the ground and comes up underneath it, and it can throw its whole bulk clear of the earth in one leap.

A headless, legless mass that slithers on a broad tapered underside and does not hold any shape long enough to describe twice. Limbs and claws surface where it needs them. Transformation magic slides off something already refusing to have a form, and its touch leaves a body unsure what shape it is meant to be.

A furred four-legged bulk with broad batlike wings and three heads set side by side at the shoulders, the last of them reptilian. That head breathes according to its colour — acid, lightning, fire or frost. Greedy, lazy and quarrelsome, it hoards whatever it kills within easy reach of where it sleeps.

A compact grey-lilac creature on two crooked legs, with arms far too long for it — rope-flexible, ending in oversized five-clawed hands. It clings above a doorway or a shaft and waits, drops its arms around a neck as someone passes underneath, and lets go the moment a fight starts going badly.

A broad rust-red crustacean on four walking legs, with two heavy pincer arms, visible gill fans and a blunt eyeless head fused into the carapace. Below the head hang four short pale tentacles whose touch leaves a body limp and aware. It senses the water and air around it well enough not to miss the lack of eyes.

A long, low-slung dragon in obsidian scale, horn-crested, with ragged wings, weathered dorsal plates and gills at the throat. It is at home in swamp water and holds its breath indefinitely, breathes a line of acid that strips flesh from bone, and is bad-tempered, secretive and unusually cruel even by the standards of its kind.

A narrow, many-segmented amber-brown crawler about the length of a hand, armoured in overlapping plates and flowing along a wall without any legs to speak of. It is blind, and hunts entirely by body heat; the hooked mandibles at the front of its head plate carry a venom that a healthy adult usually survives.

A rust-and-ochre segmented crawler roughly the length of a forearm, low and armoured, moving along walls and ceilings as readily as floors. Blind, it tracks warmth instead, and its black hooked mandibles inject a venom that leaves a grown adult weak and sweating for hours.

A thick blue-black crawler banded in copper, about as long as a man is tall, plated along its whole length and clinging to surfaces at any angle. It sees nothing at all and needs to see nothing: it follows the heat of a body, and its ivory mandibles close hard enough to reach bone.

A heavy crimson-brown crawler shielded in soot-black plate, long enough to span a room, pouring over rubble and up walls without slowing. Blind and silent, it hunts the warmth of living things, and the serrated mandibles on its broad wedge of a head take a limb as easily as they take hold.

A colossal slate-grey crawler plated in amber armour, thick through the body as a horse and long enough to ring a chamber. It registers nothing but heat, climbs anything it can grip, and the dark scissor mandibles under its shield of a head plate shear through mail without effort.

An immense dark-violet crawler under tarnished-brass shields, filling a corridor end to end and flowing along it faster than a man can run. It is blind, tracks warmth alone, and the black serrated mandibles set in its fortified head plate close on a body the way a portcullis closes on a doorway.

A titanic iron-grey crawler banded in weathered bone-white armour, long enough to bring a ceiling down by passing under it. Nothing about it can see. It reads the heat of everything alive within a considerable distance, and the blunt wedge of its head opens on mandibles that do not need venom to finish the job.

A sandy-gold scorpion about the size of a rat, walking on eight legs with a pincer on each pedipalp arm and a segmented tail arched over its back. It shelters under stone against the day's heat and stings anything that disturbs it, which is painful and occasionally worse.

A deep olive-black scorpion roughly the size of a dog, eight-legged, with amber-edged pincers and an ivory sting held ready over its back. It hunts at night by the tremor of footsteps, grips with the claws and stings once, and waits nearby for the venom to do the rest.

A rust-red scorpion the size of a large hound, running on eight legs with soot-black pincers and a pale sting curled above the body. Cold-blooded and unhurried, it lies up in shade or ruin through the day and works by night, and it will take on prey considerably larger than itself.

A cobalt-black scorpion as big as a pony, eight-legged, with bronze-edged pincers heavy enough to hold a struggling adult still and a red-brown sting arched over its back. It hears movement through the ground long before it sees anything, and it does not startle or retreat.

A bone-grey scorpion with tar-black joints, larger than a warhorse, its bone-white pincers wide enough to close around a torso and its obsidian sting riding high over the whole armoured mass. It feels footfalls through the rock and is on them before the sound arrives.

A crimson-and-obsidian scorpion the size of a cottage, walking on eight legs with enormous black pincers and a brass-coloured sting held over the whole assembly. It takes cattle without effort and a mounted rider not much harder, and it feels an approach through the ground long before it arrives.

A scorpion of volcanic basalt colouring seamed with sulfur yellow, big enough to straddle a road, with iron-black pincers and an ivory sting arched far above the ground. There is nothing subtle about it and nothing local that can fight it. It simply walks in and eats.

An immense segmented worm, blind and eyeless, boring through solid rock on nothing but muscle and appetite. It smells and feels its way, swallows whatever it meets whole, and digests bone, iron and stone alike. A tunnel of the right diameter is the only warning anyone usually gets.

A robust amber-and-black bee grown to the size of a large dog, with four wings, two antennae and a barbed sting on the abdomen. It works flowers as any bee does and ignores passers-by unless the hive is threatened, at which point the whole hive is the problem, not the one bee.

A lean carmine-and-charcoal wasp with a narrow waist, hooked mandibles and a long ivory sting, big enough to carry off a small animal. Unlike its cousin the bee it is a hunter, and it paralyses prey to stock a nest rather than killing it outright.

A lean flying reptile with two clawed hind legs, short forearms and broad membranous wings, its long tail ending in a barbed sting. It hunts alone and from height, dropping onto prey and driving the sting home; the venom will kill an animal its own size. It is bestial rather than clever.

A spider-shaped horror in charcoal and carmine armour, headless in the sense that its body and skull are one fused shell, walking on six taloned legs with a swollen spinneret behind. It leaps far further than its bulk suggests, webs what it hunts, and prefers to hunt its own kind.

A single sheet of charcoal leather with no head and no limbs, hanging against a ceiling until it reads as nothing more than a discarded cloak. It drops onto whatever passes beneath, wraps it, and works a pale crescent mouth against it, while a subsonic moan pulls the shadows in the room out of true.

A ridiculous-looking bird the size of a large goose: rooster's head and crimson comb on a compact feathered body, two clawed legs, two small wings, and a long green-black serpent's tail. Nothing about it is dangerous except the beak, and the beak turns whatever it breaks the skin of to stone.

A long serpent in turquoise and gold with two vast feathered wings and a horn-crested head. It is old, genuinely wise, and considerably more intelligent than most of what it speaks to. It coils and constricts when it must fight, but it would far rather talk, and it usually gets what it wants that way.

A charcoal-violet bell of leather with eight short hooked tendrils and a ring of teeth underneath, which hangs from a cavern ceiling looking exactly like a stalactite. It is blind and navigates by echo. It drops, smothers a head, and floods the area with darkness so nobody can see to help.

An immense slug plated in moss-green and copper mineral crust, with two broad paddle arms ending in blunt obsidian claws and a ridged sensory disk where a face would be. It eats stone and metal, dissolving a passage as it goes, and leaves smooth-walled tunnels that betray it long after it has moved on.

An ember-black giant of a fiend, horned and wreathed in heat, with vast smoke-dark wings, an obsidian greatsword in one hand and a flaming whip in the other. It is fast, clever and magnificently persuasive when it chooses. Most of what threatens it is destroyed before it has finished speaking.

A squat, warted thing with a broad head sunk into its shoulders, a potbelly, bowed legs and long claws. It is stupid, cowardly, and only ever encountered in numbers, because individually it is worth nothing to anyone — including whatever drove it up here.

A towering hyena-headed fiend with four arms — two ending in heavy pincers, two in clawed hands — standing on reverse-jointed legs. It is intelligent, patient and fond of offering people exactly what they asked for. The pincers are for when the negotiation is over.

A massive toad-headed brute in pebbled charcoal-olive hide, neckless, crouching on thick webbed-taloned legs. It reeks badly enough to turn a stomach at a distance, has no patience whatsoever, and settles most disagreements by getting hold of someone and biting.

A bronze-skinned torso with six arms rising from the coils of a crimson-and-black serpent's body. Each hand holds a blade and each blade is used well; what it cannot cut it wraps and crushes. It commands other fiends, thinks like a general, and enjoys none of it in any way a person would recognise.

A mountain of a fiend, boar-headed and tusked, its ape-shaped torso sagging over short legs that end in split black hooves. It is lazy, gluttonous and vain, and considerably more dangerous than any of that suggests once it decides that getting up is worth the effort.

A headless oval of black iron on four long walking legs, with four shorter scythe arms folded against the body and mandibles set in the front rim. It is a hunting machine built to fetch one named thing, it does not stop, and it cannot be reasoned with because there is nothing in it to reason with.

A poised figure with ember-brown skin, long black hair and subtle black claws, showing no horns, wings or tail unless it suits them to. The danger is never the claws. It is the conversation: they read what you want, offer it, and collect on the arrangement long after you have stopped noticing one was made.

A bald vulture-headed fiend on digitigrade bird legs, with muscular clawed arms and broad ragged wings. It is spiteful and greedy and fights in a screeching flurry — the screech itself is a weapon, leaving anyone nearby stunned and easy to open up.

A small, long-bodied hunter on four short legs, narrow-headed and endlessly flexible, able to follow prey down a hole barely wider than its skull. It is playful in a way that reads as cruelty and kills animals rather larger than itself.

The same long, low, flexible build as a common weasel, scaled up to the size of a horse, with a broad mustelid head, amber eyes and long ivory canines. It latches on and drinks, and it keeps the smaller kind's habit of killing well past the point of any need for food.

A low, broad, striped digger on four short powerful legs with heavy blunt claws. It wants to be left alone and will say so; if it is not left alone it goes berserk and keeps fighting well past the point where any sensible animal would have run.

A barrel-bodied digger the size of a pony, silver-striped and scarred, on pillar-thick legs ending in oversized claws. It has all the smaller badger's temper and none of its limits: once it starts, it does not disengage, does not tire quickly, and does not appear to feel much.

Three tons of grey hide on four pillar legs, with a single long nasal horn and small eyes that see very little. It goes through thorn scrub without noticing it. Startled, it charges whatever it thinks caused the noise, and it does not need to be right about that.

A compact, pale-violet humanoid barely four feet tall, with oversized eyes that cannot bear daylight. They move quietly, fight with a short blade and a light crossbow, and pursue elaborate cruelties for reasons that make complete sense to them and none to anyone else.

An eyeless armoured biped on four clawed legs, its wedge of a head flanked by two enormous ribbed membrane fans and fronted by a ring of resonating teeth. It hears with extraordinary precision and attacks with sound alone, tuned to shatter stone, gear or the inside of a body as it prefers.

A lump of wax-red flesh in the rough shape of a person, neckless and legless, dragging itself forward on two overlong arms with a silent toothless mouth working. There is no mind left in it and no will of its own. It goes where it is sent and stops when it is destroyed.

A tall, skeletal figure of bone plate and dry sinew, ember-eyed, with a long segmented tail ending in a sting. It is a jailer and an interrogator by temperament, deeply unpleasant to be near, and it works patiently to find the thing you will not give up.

A broad rust-black fiend covered head to foot in long spines, with oversized clawed hands and a low wedge of a head. Grappling it is a mistake; so is standing close. It is suspicious of everything, guards what it has been given to guard, and never quite believes the relief is coming.

A striking figure in dark bronze lamellar with broad soot-black feathered wings, carrying a longsword and a bow whose arrows take fire in flight. It also carries a rope, which is the part to worry about: it prefers its quarry bound and delivered rather than killed.

A lion-sized cat in ash-grey fur with ember eyes and a long whip of a tail, visible only as a shimmer of outline in daylight and perfectly plain in the dark. It hunts by scent, moves in silence, and is far cleverer about ambush than an animal of its shape has any right to be.

A charcoal-scaled fiend with two long swept-back bronze horns, rust-red batlike wings and a heavy armoured tail, carrying a length of barbed chain. It is a shock troop and a bully, heals what you do to it, and fights with the confidence of something that has done this many times.

An insectoid fiend a head taller than any man, faceted-eyed and mandibled, with reverse-jointed legs ending in ice hooks and a long segmented tail. Cold comes off it in a wave. It carries a spear, thinks carefully before it uses it, and commands whatever lesser fiends are to hand.

The worst thing in the hierarchy that still takes a recognisable shape: obsidian-scaled, crown-horned, furnace-eyed, with enormous crimson-black wings and a barbed tail. It is as clever as any archmage and rather older, it heals faster than most things can cut, and it never fights a battle it has not already arranged.

A long, low armoured predator in ochre and slate on four clawed legs, with a small weak-toothed mouth and a swollen throat sac it does not use for calling. The sac holds acid, which it sprays in a cone hot enough to strip a body down, then laps up what remains.

In its own shape, a lean, hairless, pearl-grey humanoid with large silver eyes and six-fingered hands — a shape almost nobody sees. It reads the surface of a mind and wears the result, and it is good enough at being someone else that the people closest to them do not notice.

A long, low dragon in moss-green scale with leaf-veined wings and a narrow wedge of a head, at home in old forest and equally at home under water. It breathes a cloud of acid. It is the schemer of its kind: it would rather corrupt, bargain and manoeuvre than fight, and it is very good at it.

A desert dragon in cobalt and sand scale with a single long ivory horn on its forehead and storm-grey wings. It breathes lightning in a straight line, burrows through dune and hardpan to lie in wait, and is vain, orderly and territorial to a degree that surprises people expecting a mere animal.

A heavy forest primate in short charcoal-brown fur, barrel-chested, with very long arms, grasping feet and no tail. It moves through the canopy faster than anyone can follow on the ground, and it is strong enough and short-tempered enough that treating it as harmless is a mistake people make once.

A dog-muzzled monkey in olive-brown fur with amber eyes, long arms and a long tail, at home on rock faces and in trees alike. It travels in troops, bullies anything smaller, and will mob a lone traveller who looks like they are carrying food.

A small golden-brown monkey with a dark face, bright eyes and a prehensile tail longer than the rest of it. It goes through a canopy faster than anything on the ground can track, steals whatever is not tied down, and bites when cornered.

A vast iron-grey primate, barrel-chested, with pillar-thick arms scarred from use and pale amber eyes. It swings through heavy timber as easily as its smaller cousins and hits with force enough to end a fight in one blow. Bad-tempered, and very hard to discourage.

A long, low cat in golden tan patterned with black rosettes, built for the single explosive rush. It hunts alone, drags a kill up a tree to eat undisturbed, and is on a target from cover before most people register that the cover was occupied.
A tawny cat the size of a draught horse, dark-maned, moving with the same patient economy as a lion a tenth its weight. It hears a heartbeat across a clearing. What it pins does not get up again.

Two tons of burnt-orange and black stripe, and in broken light almost impossible to see until it moves. It stalks in near silence, closes the last stretch in a rush, and takes hold with both front paws before the jaws do anything at all.

A low barrel of charcoal-brown muscle with pale shoulder bands and oversized digging claws, about the size of a bear and far worse tempered. It climbs, it does not retreat, and it will drive a much larger predator off a kill by sheer refusal to stop.

A compact, muscular dark-bay pony trained not to bolt at noise, blood or steel. It carries a rider all day, kicks with real intent, and holds its ground in a line where an untrained animal would already be gone.

A squat olive-brown toad with warty skin and copper eyes, sitting perfectly still against wet leaf litter until something small enough to swallow comes past. Entirely harmless to anyone larger than a beetle.

A high-shouldered dark-brown grazer with a woolly forequarter coat and short curved black horns. Placid in the ordinary way of cattle and completely unmanageable once a herd starts moving; the danger is rarely the one animal.

A charcoal-furred bat with a wingspan wide enough to fill a corridor, huge pointed ears and a mouth of fine sharp teeth. It navigates by sound in complete darkness, hunts on the wing, and is far more startling than it is deadly.

A high-shouldered bear in dense frost-tipped umber fur, weighing as much as a loaded cart, standing up to better than twice a man's height. It is short-tempered, hard to put down, and hits with a paw wide enough to take a shield with the arm behind it.

A bristling, high-shouldered boar with two huge ivory tusks and small hostile eyes. It charges first and considers nothing afterwards, keeps coming with wounds that would drop most animals, and is at its most dangerous when it should already be dead.

A slate-grey shark long enough to swallow a rowing boat's crew one at a time, blunt-headed, with a mouth of triangular teeth set in rows. It tastes blood across a great distance of water and arrives without any warning at all.

An enormous mottled blue-grey whale with a pleated throat and a mouth that strains its food from the water rather than biting it. It is not a predator of anything larger than a shrimp, but a ship that gets under one when it breaches has a serious problem.

A blunt-headed, deeply scarred whale with a narrow toothed lower jaw, diving further than anything else that breathes to fight squid in the dark. It is the largest hunter in the water, and the scars on it were made by things most sailors never see.

A black-and-white hunter with a tall triangular fin, fast, sociable and disturbingly clever. Orcas work in coordinated groups, talk while they do it, and take prey considerably larger than themselves by having agreed a plan beforehand.

A charcoal-grey diamond of a fish, wider than a man is tall, flying through open water on two enormous triangular wings. Its whip of a tail carries no barb and it eats nothing bigger than plankton; it is startling to meet and harmless to almost everything.
A slender bronze-olive lizard the length of a hand, quick over hot stone and quick to freeze when watched. It swims when it has to, eats insects, and drops its tail rather than be caught by it.

A heavy ochre-brown lizard the size of a large dog, bow-legged, with a flicking forked tongue and a long muscular tail it uses like a club. It tastes the air to track carrion or prey, digs, climbs, swims, and eats considerably more than seems reasonable.

Ten yards of armoured olive-black reptile lying just under the waterline with only two amber eyes showing. It is patient beyond any mammal's endurance, takes hold with a jaw that does not open again, and rolls to finish what it has caught.

A sloping, high-shouldered scavenger in coarse spotted fur with a jaw that cracks bone for the marrow. It runs in packs, follows better hunters to steal from them, and is bolder around a campfire at night than anyone expects.

A low, heavily muscled mastiff bred to carry a small rider or pull a load, sable and cream, with folded ears and a strong jaw. Loyal, greedy, and perfectly willing to go at something much larger than itself if told to.

A golden-brown raptor with a hooked ivory beak and yellow taloned feet, able to pick out movement on the ground from a height where it is barely a speck itself. It stoops fast enough that small prey never hears it coming.

A glossy black bird with a heavy beak and an unsettlingly knowing eye. Ravens remember faces, work out latches and lids, take shiny things for no clear reason, and follow armies because they have learned what armies leave behind.

A rust-red mantle and eight sucker-lined arms around a hidden beak, with two horizontal-pupilled eyes that watch far more carefully than they ought to. It changes colour to match stone in a heartbeat, squeezes through any gap its beak fits, and would much rather hide than fight.

An olive-violet mantle the size of a hay bale trailing eight colossal sucker-lined arms. It matches the rock it is lying against until it moves, takes hold of a limb or a hull with several arms at once, and pulls what it holds down towards the beak.

A tapered blue-grey torpedo with two fins at the rear, eight short arms around a hidden beak and two longer feeding tentacles that snap out and back. It swims fast, in shoals, and flees far more readily than it attacks.

A charcoal-red hunter of the deep water, its mantle longer than a boat, with huge pale eyes, eight muscular arms and two long feeding tentacles ending in toothed clubs. It takes hold from below and out of the dark, and it is strong enough to argue with a whale.

The archetype the word conjures: crimson scale, black swept-back horns, furnace-gold eyes, soot-dark wings and a barbed tail. It breathes fire and it never sleeps. Vain, cruel and covetous past any sense, it takes what it wants, keeps it, and remembers who tried to take it back.

A polished-brass desert dragon with broad brow horns, a fan of flat cheek scales and a spade-tipped tail. It breathes fire, or a sleeping gas when it wants a problem to go away quietly. It is a relentless talker and would genuinely rather hear your news than eat you.

A dark-bronze coastal dragon with sea-green eyes, webbed toes, a ribbed crest and a finned tail, as much at home under water as above it. It breathes lightning, and a gas that pushes attackers back rather than killing them. It likes ships, sailors and a just war.

A hammered-copper dragon of hills and dry rock, turquoise-eyed, with a crown of flat stone-like scales and a chisel-bladed tail. It climbs anything, breathes acid, and can slow a pursuer to a crawl with a gas. It is a compulsive joker and takes losing very badly.

An elegant dragon in pearl-silver with midnight-blue horns, ice-blue eyes and a lance-tipped tail, at ease in cloud and high cold air. It breathes killing frost, or a gas that leaves attackers rigid and unhurt. Of all its kind it is the one most inclined to walk among people.

The greatest of the metal dragons: red-gold, ivory-horned, molten-amber eyes above a sunburst crest of scales, with crimson-gold wings and a leaf-bladed tail. It breathes fire, and a gas that saps the strength out of anyone still standing. Old, formidable, and genuinely just.

A dark-teal draconic head and four paddle limbs emerging from a domed shell the size of a hill, bronze-edged and black-green. It lies on a sea floor or a deep river bed for years at a time, and it breathes a jet of scalding steam that empties a deck.

A lion's body and gait under irregular brass scales, with a rust-gold mane, a draconic head and small swept-back brow ridges. It has no wings and does not miss them. Its roar is loud enough to leave anyone nearby unsteady on their feet.

A pale-violet humanoid torso rising from the black-violet body of a great spider, moving on eight jointed legs. It keeps its hands free for a bow and a dagger, spins and climbs as readily as it walks, and is bitter about what it used to be.

A slender figure whose skin runs into bark and whose hair is a crown of oak leaves and fine twigs, carrying a longbow and a dagger. She is bound to one particular tree and cannot go far from it; harm the tree and the woodland stops being neutral about you.

A golden-brown eagle with a wingspan that shades a cart, an ivory beak and talons that close on a deer. Unlike a common raptor it speaks, keeps its word, and takes a considered view of who is worth carrying and who is worth dropping.

A copper-skinned figure with wind-tossed dark hair, in layered indigo, sand and weathered brass, carrying a falchion at the hip and a bow across the back. Quick-tempered and quicker to act, it holds to its own code absolutely and to nobody else's rules at all.

A dark-skinned figure with close-cropped silver hair, in moon-silver plate over deep violet cloth, holding an incandescent greatsword in both hands. It gives off its own light. It can set the armour aside entirely and go as a globe of that light instead, which is when it is hardest to fight.

A two-headed giant in patched furs, grey-brown and filthy, with a crude iron-studded club in each hand. The heads argue constantly and never both sleep, so it is almost impossible to surprise, and it fights both hands at once without either getting in the other's way.

A bounded cyclone of pearl-grey and silver wind with the suggestion of a face near the top and two gusting arms below it, tapering to a narrow vortex instead of legs. There is nothing solid in it to cut. It buffets, it lifts, and it goes wherever the air can.

A squat body of interlocked slate, granite and ochre clay, with a boulder for a head and blunt fists in place of hands. It walks through solid rock as easily as a person walks through a doorway, and it hits like the wall it stepped out of.

A spiral core of white-hot, orange and deep-red flame with two curling arms and two trailing legs, casting light on everything nearby. Everything it touches catches. Water is the answer to it, and the only reliable one.

A coiling core of deep blue and turquoise water, foam-edged, with two flexible pseudopods for arms and two streams trailing where legs would be. It is impossible to hold and nearly impossible to hurt in its own element, and it drags what it catches under.

A narrow blue-grey pear of a body with no head at all, a mouth opening in its front, four double-jointed arms and a single muscular leg it balances on. It steps sideways out of the world, takes one specific thing you were carrying, and steps back out again.

A cobalt-violet predator on four running legs, low and flexible, with pearly ridges down its back and a mouth of small sharp teeth. It hunts from just outside the world, arriving beside its prey with no approach to hear and leaving the same way when the meal is over.

A hunched, carapaced humanoid in bark-brown and charcoal, with a cluster of small black eyes and two short fangs. It keeps spiders the way a farmer keeps dogs, strings the approaches to its lair with web and deadfall, and prefers a victim already tangled.

A vast segmented worm sheathed in blue-white ice armour, eyeless, with a ring of fangs opening directly in the front of its body. It lies buried in snow, indistinguishable from a drift, and breathes a cold that kills outright. Its trilling call leaves anything that hears it standing still and stupid.

A violet-black mushroom the height of a man, pale-gilled underneath, rooted in cave floor and utterly inert. It is blind, deaf and harmless. What it does is notice movement and light nearby and scream about it, until whatever else lives down there arrives to see why.

A folded purple cap on a mottled grey-violet stalk, indistinguishable from ordinary cave fungus until the four long tentacles come out. Their touch rots flesh where it lands. It grows in stands, often among shriekers, which is not a coincidence.

A slate-grey stone figure with short backward horns, blunt claws, batlike wings and a tapering tail, perched motionless on a ledge among ordinary carvings. It can hold that stillness for days. It neither eats nor breathes; it waits, and it hurts things for entertainment.

The gargoyle's seagoing cousin: water-worn blue-grey basalt, a single brow horn, webbed hands and feet and a flattened swimming tail in place of wings. It lies among rocks on a harbour bottom looking like ballast, and takes swimmers from below.

A towering sky-blue figure with swept-back cloud-white hair, in white and indigo, standing on the ground like anyone else. It is proud, generous when well treated, and capable of stepping between worlds and taking company with it. Coercion goes badly for the person attempting it.

A cobalt-blue figure in ivory and royal purple with a swept-back white mane and a plain circlet, carrying rank the way other people carry a weapon. It commands lesser djinn, travels between worlds at will, and expects to be addressed properly.

An enormous ember-red figure seamed with glowing fissures, black volcanic hair swept back above a hard face, standing on obsidian feet. It bargains with genuine enthusiasm and honours the letter of every agreement precisely, which is the trap. Water is what it fears.

The genie that lives in the world rather than visiting it: bronze-skinned, black-braided, in practical sand and copper armour with a falchion and a bow. Jann keep to deserts and wastes, trade honestly enough, and can step to another plane briefly when they have to.

An eagle's head, beak and taloned forelegs on a tawny lion's body, with broad golden-brown wings and a tufted tail. It is an animal, not a speaker, and a bad-tempered one. It hunts horses by preference, which makes it a problem for anyone travelling mounted.

A hairless cadaver-grey corpse in tatters of burial cloth, hunched, with an elongated jaw and clawed hands. It stinks, animals bolt from it, and its hunger for the dead does not distinguish between the recently dead and the nearly so.

A waterlogged blue-grey ghoul in rags of sailcloth, webbed at hand and foot, that hunts drowned coast and harbour bottom instead of graveyards. It takes wreck survivors and swimmers, and it does not need to surface to do it.

A taller, stronger ghoul in ash-black, with raised bony shoulder ridges and the same elongated jaw. The stench off it is bad enough to stop a fighter mid-swing, and unlike the common sort it is not turned away by the usual protections.

A milky sky-blue giant with long silver-white hair, dressed in white, pale blue and brass with real care. It lives high enough that thin air is no trouble, has excellent hearing, a fine sense of smell and a weakness for a wager, and throws stones the size of a barrel.

A charcoal-black giant with bright orange hair under an open-faced blackened helm, in half plate over red and black cloth. Fire does not mark it; cold does. It is a disciplined soldier by temperament and works iron better than most smiths alive.

A lean ice-blue giant with long pale hair under a plain helm, in layered hides, dark pelts and chain. Cold is nothing to it and fire is worse than it should be. It raids from high country, takes what it needs, and respects very little except strength.

A wiry slate-grey giant with faint granite mottling, in thick brown-and-grey leather. It keeps to itself and dislikes being looked at, presses flat against a cliff and becomes part of it, and throws a rock with genuinely alarming accuracy.

A violet-skinned giant with long blue-black hair and a silver headband, gill-slit at the neck, in a loose blue-grey tunic. It breathes water as readily as air, lightning does nothing to it, and it is the largest and most thoughtful of all the giant kinds.

A low mound of wet ochre and bruised violet protoplasm with six flesh stalks rising out of it, each ending in a toothed mouth. All six talk at once, and the babble makes it very hard to think straight near it. It spits acid and it flows rather than walks.

A heavy white-furred ape with four arms, fanged, standing on two broad charcoal feet. It swings through canopy on all four hands, grabs with two while it uses the others, and comes down on prey from above without warning.

A smoothly articulated body of dark forged iron with integrated armour and a sealed, featureless helm — no eyes, no mouth, nothing to read. Spells break on it. It does not tire, does not stop, and does exactly what its last instruction said.

A blocky granite figure with a shallow, featureless face and carved armour ridges, standing motionless until something crosses whatever line it was given. Magic slides off it and blades chip against it. It is slow, and it does not need to be fast.

The same faceless basalt guardian built on an architectural scale, tall enough to reach a second storey, with layered armour ridges cut into it. Everything true of the smaller kind is true of this one, and there is a great deal more of it.

A bull the size of a small cart, plated head to hoof in overlapping dark iron scale, with heavy forward-curving horns. It charges anything that enters its ground. What it breathes out is not smoke: whatever is caught in the cloud stops moving permanently.

A hunched slate-grey biped in thick wrinkled hide, with six small amber eyes across its brow and four-fingered clawed hands. It is enormously strong and inclined to tear rather than kill cleanly. Oddly, it will attach itself to one creature it has decided to guard, and defend it to the end.

A long rubbery charcoal-brown worm with no limbs, its front ringed by four flexible tentacles around a small sharp beak. It clings to a tunnel wall or ceiling looking like wet rock, drops on whatever passes, and drags the remains back to the same crevice.

A stocky dull-grey humanoid whose brow is smooth and sealed where eyes should be, with prominent ears and a broad nose that do the work instead. It knows its own caverns perfectly, fights with an axe, and eats what it kills, including people.

An eagle-headed figure whose forelimbs are its wings, with a small five-fingered hand at each wing's wrist and long raptor legs beneath. Its eyesight is extraordinary even by its own standards. It speaks with animals, sees through invisibility, and will not harm the innocent.

An upright lion in short tawny-gold fur with a dense dark mane, clawed at hand and foot, with a tufted tail. It leaps enormous distances, roars loudly enough to be a weapon in itself, and hunts fiends with the straightforwardness of something that has never needed a plan.

A towering hag with cold slate-blue skin like weathered iron, stringy black hair, a fanged mouth and arms far too long for the rest of her. She schemes as a matter of course, keeps to bargains she has actually made, and crushes what she gets hold of.

A gaunt hag in mottled olive-green skin with tangled reed-black hair, pointed ears and gill slits at the neck. She lives in fen and river bottom, breathes water, mimics any voice she has heard, and would far rather manipulate someone into ruin than fight them for it.

A hag covered in overlapping blue-grey and kelp-green scale, with pale sea-glass eyes, finlike ears and gill frills at the throat. She lives alone in cold water and is hideous enough that the sight of her can stop a heart outright. Her stare does the rest.

A weathered woman's head and torso on birdlike legs with taloned feet, wings of brown and ash feathers growing from her back and a club in one hand. The danger is the singing: it is genuinely beautiful, it carries a long way, and people walk into her reach smiling.

A lean coal-black hound with ember-orange eyes and a mouth that glows with contained heat, faint red cracks showing through short fur. Its bite burns as it closes, it can breathe a gout of fire, and it hunts in packs with more coordination than a wolf.

A hell hound bred up to the size of a draught horse, coal-black, mailed across the chest and shoulders in dark infernal links. Its jaws glow with the same heat and it breathes the same fire, but this one is a mount and a war beast, and it comes with a rider.

An eagle's head, chest and taloned forelegs joined to the body and hind legs of a dun horse, with broad brown-and-cream wings. It is a straightforward animal, easier to train than a griffon, and it fights readily to defend its nest.

A hand-high clay figure with an oversized head, long pointed ears, small leathery wings and a mouth of tiny fangs, still showing its maker's sculpting marks. It shares its creator's mind at any distance, and it does not outlive them.

A muscular blue-grey scaled humanoid with a wide toothed mouth, lidless pale eyes, gill slits and webbed clawed hands, carrying a long spear. It breathes water and air alike. It was made to serve something else, and it is still doing so.

A pearl-grey horse with a flowing silver mane and enormous white-and-silver wings. It is an animal, not a speaker, but a clever and famously particular one: it chooses its own riders and cannot be broken into accepting a different answer.

A tawny-brown owl the size of a horse, with a wide facial disk, amber eyes and a hooked beak. It flies in complete silence — the first anyone knows of it is the talons. It talks, keeps its own counsel, and dislikes noisy company.

A long ash-grey quadruped with a huge toothed mouth and a mane of black-and-ivory quills over neck and shoulders. It sheds those quills into whatever it claws. Its howl carries for miles and wears down the nerve of anyone who has to keep listening to it.

A low grey-brown reptile the size of a barn on four crocodilian legs, with five serpentine necks rising from its shoulders and a fanged head on each. Every head watches a different direction, all of them bite in the same round, and none of them can be crept up on.

A hydra in dark red and charcoal scale with ember seams showing between the plates. Five heads, five sets of fangs, and each of them can breathe fire. Fire will not hurt it back, so the usual answer to a many-headed problem does not apply here.

A deep-purple hydra with pale lavender scales rimed at the edges with frost, its five heads breathing killing cold rather than biting alone. It keeps to high or northern country, and it is no less willing than its warmer cousins to use every head at once.

Eight feet of living air, weighing almost nothing and visible to nobody. It is bound to a task and follows it without rest across any distance, and it resents both the binding and whoever did the binding. What it hits, it hits out of empty room.

A clockwork figure in dark steel banded mail, gold and silver, with glowing golden eyes and gears turning visibly beneath the plate. It carries a very fine longsword and it exists to enforce bargains. If you broke a contract, it already knows the terms.

A colossal construct of black stone and gold in integrated full plate, carrying no weapon because its fists are the weapon. It comes for those who have cheated death, it does not negotiate, and the sound of it arriving is generally the last warning given.

A gold-and-silver centaur of clockwork, armoured above and equine below, with broad metal wings and a spiked chain coiled at each forearm. It hunts fugitives from justice across any distance and hands them back alive where it can.

A blue-black mantle the size of a warship with green-gold eyes, trailing six grasping arms and two much longer barbed hunting tentacles around a central beak. It is old, patient and genuinely intelligent. It takes ships apart at leisure and eats the crew afterwards.

A lean tawny-grey cat about the size of a large hound, narrow-headed, with swept-back ears. Its trick is to peel the skin of its face back over its skull, which is horrifying enough to break a line, and it hunts in family groups that use the effect deliberately.

A black-haired woman from the waist up and a tawny lion below, moving on four clawed paws with a dagger in hand. She is a liar by preference and a cruel one, and considerably stronger than the human half of her suggests.

A golden lion's body with enormous bronze-gold wings and the head of a dark-haired man, amber-eyed and grave. It guards old sites and older obligations, breathes fire when pressed to it, and speaks with anyone willing to be reasonable first.

A copper-haired woman's head and torso on an iridescent blue-teal serpent's body, with broad rainbow-feathered wings. She is an artist before she is anything else — musician, poet, painter — and she guards wild places and the works made in them.

A lean yellow-green scaled fish-person with pearl eyes, neck gill fans and a crest running from crown to back, carrying a long spear. They live in organised communities on the sea floor, trade when approached properly, and fight well in defence of their own.

A squat figure of cracked black volcanic rock with magma showing in the fissures, about four feet tall and giving off light. It sets fire to whatever it touches and does so with obvious delight; it starts fires for no reason beyond wanting to watch them.

A russet lion's body with dark red-brown batlike wings and a broad, unsettlingly humanlike maned head. The tail ends in a dense fan of black spikes it throws in volleys from the air, and it is clever enough to do that from out of reach and wait.

A humanoid whose scalp carries a crown of short living serpents, each with its own head and its own bite. They keep their eyes veiled or averted in company and prefer a bow at a distance, because anyone who meets that gaze directly turns to stone where they stand.

A living cloud of hundreds of cave bats pouring out of a ceiling crack in a spiral. Individually they are nothing; together they fill the room, foul torches, tangle in hair and armour, and make it impossible to see or hear anything useful.

A vortex of thumb-sized infernal wasps that behaves less like insects and more like one thing with a plan. Fire does not disperse it. It flows through gaps in armour, and it can occupy a body and walk it around long after the occupant has stopped agreeing.

A swirling carpet of rats, hundreds of them, moving as one across a cellar floor. Weapons accomplish very little against it. It goes up clothing and under mail, it carries whatever the last corpse had, and it does not care how many of it you kill.

A skinny pale-blue imp with long swept ears, clawed hands and cloud-white wings, its lower body trailing off into a curl of moving air instead of legs. It is nosy, cowardly and constantly talking, and it spits a blast of stinging grit before fleeing.

A thin ochre-grey mephit of cracked dried clay with dust-brown leathery wings. Everything about it sheds fine powder. It breathes a choking cloud of it, and the mess it leaves in a room lasts long after the mephit has lost interest.

A compact mephit of layered slate and granite with heavy stone wings that ought not to work and do anyway. It is the slowest and sturdiest of its kind, presses itself against rock and vanishes into it, and spits a burst of grit and splinters.

A skinny coal-black mephit lit ember-orange at the joints, with crimson-shot leathery wings and sharp claws. It is spiteful, easily offended, and breathes a short gout of flame at anything that has annoyed it, which is most things.

A faceted mephit of pale blue ice with frost-white rime wings, cold enough to hurt to stand beside. It breathes a spray of shards, it is as brittle as it looks in places, and it is easily the most sneering of a family not known for manners.

A mephit of cracked black basalt glowing orange inside its fissures, with heavy stone wings veined the same colour. It gives off enough light to read by and enough heat to blister, and what it breathes out is a spatter of molten rock.

A dark, slick mephit of dense ooze and wet clay with fin-shaped ears and dripping teal wings. It smells appalling, it slips out of any grip, and it leaves behind a cloud thick enough to empty a room of everyone still able to walk.

A chalk-white mephit of salt crystal veined with pale rose, with heavy halite wings. It is drier than anything nearby has any right to be, cracks audibly when struck, and breathes a burst of crystals that draws the water out of whatever they land on.

A pale pewter-grey mephit seamed with copper heat lines, its wings clouded with vapour trapped inside the membrane. It is the most self-important of the family, and it breathes scalding steam at anyone who fails to take it seriously.

In its resting shape, a heavy iron-banded chest of dark oak, indistinguishable from the real thing until the lid seam opens into a mouth. Two adhesive pseudopods come out of the sides and take hold, and once stuck to it a person is not simply pulling free.

A bull-headed humanoid half again the height of a tall man, furred, heavily muscled, with two long forward-curving horns and cloven hooves. It never loses its bearings underground however tangled the passages run, and it fights with horns, claws and a great axe cut to its own reach.

An eyeless dead-grey corpse of exposed ribs and blackened sinew, with a long dark-red barbed tongue rooted in a broken mouth. It was a murderer in life and is still one. The tongue is what to watch: its touch leaves a body rigid and entirely awake.

A desiccated body wound tightly in dried wrappings, moving with the deliberateness of something that has nowhere else to be. Nothing frightens it, nothing distracts it from what it was set to guard, and it burns better than it should.

A charcoal-scaled serpent as long as a cart, hooded like a cobra, with a woman's face set into the hood and violet eyes. It reads the surface of a mind while it talks, which makes lying to it pointless, and it kills with fangs and a stinging tail.

An emerald-scaled hooded serpent with a calm human face and gold eyes, coiled where it has chosen to stand watch. It is patient, well-intentioned and hard to move, spits venom with real accuracy, and would much rather warn someone off than kill them.

An oxblood-scaled serpent with a gaunt, hideous human face in its hood and ember eyes, and a smell about it that turns a stomach. Meeting its gaze leaves a person compliant and pleased about it, which is how most of its victims arrive.

A cobalt-scaled sea serpent with a human face and pearl-blue eyes, ringed with short spines. It is curious about strangers and short-tempered about being handled, breathes water, and coils around what it means to keep hold of.

A wiry blue-black crone with coarse iron-grey hair, pointed ears and long black claws, wearing a dark red heartstone on an iron chain. She walks into sleep the way other people walk into a room, and rides a sleeper night after night until there is nothing left to ride.

A black horse with a mane of red-orange flame and fire cuffing each hoof, leaving scorch marks where it stands. It flies, it does not tire, and it trails a choking smoke that blinds anyone trying to close with its rider.

The greater nightmare: an obsidian-black warhorse of enormous mass, crimson-maned in flame, each pillar leg ending in a hoof ringed with white-orange fire. Everything the lesser kind does, this one does harder, and it carries something worse than a rider often enough.

An enormous eyeless worm of matte black and midnight-violet corpse plate, boring through the earth with a crescent of teeth at the front and a recurved stinger at the tail. Living things nearby simply stop being alive. It is as clever as any general and entirely dead.

A gaunt black giant, hairless and featureless, with very long arms ending in blunt crushing claws, drifting rather than walking. It puts out life around it the way cold puts out a candle, and it is intelligent enough to make that a strategy.

A vast black bat of solid darkness, silent on the wing, hunting by night above whatever it has decided to empty. Living things wither where its shadow passes. It thinks, it plans, and it is very hard to see coming.

A fey of a wild spring or grove, beautiful past what a person is built to look at directly — a moment of eye contact leaves someone standing helpless. She is impulsive, easily bored, deeply attached to her own patch of country, and dangerous mainly to those who will not leave it alone.

A shapeless mass of viscous black matter that pours along walls and ceilings as easily as floors, and weighs several tons. It is blind, mindless and entirely without organs, so there is nothing on it to aim at; what it flows over, it digests.

A sheet of wet grey sludge that looks exactly like wet stone until it moves, spread across a floor or seeping down a wall. It is blind and mindless, feels neither heat nor cold, and dissolves what it settles on at its own unhurried pace.

A translucent yellow-brown mass several tons in weight, flowing over stone and squeezing through cracks far narrower than itself. It has no eyes, no mind and nothing that can be reasoned with; it simply arrives, spreads, and digests.

A transparent cube of dense jelly, wider than the corridor it fills and nearly invisible until light catches an edge. It sweeps passages at a walking pace, digesting everything organic it engulfs and carrying the indigestible — coins, buckles, blades — suspended inside it as it goes.

A bear-bodied predator with the head, beak and fixed staring eyes of a great owl, feathered across the shoulders and heavy enough to put a horse down. It has neither fear nor patience, attacks on sight, and will follow a fleeing meal well past the point where a bear would lose interest.

A squat, many-tendrilled fungus that walks on stubby legs and cannot be seen at all — the invisibility is permanent and natural to it. Deaf and near-mindless, it blunders through caverns eating what it catches, and it catches things that never knew it was there.

A large spider that spends most of its time slightly outside the world. It steps in beside its prey, bites, and steps back out before a weapon can answer — the venom does the work while the spider waits somewhere nothing can reach it.

In its true form a shapeless mass that flows rather than walks, with a single pseudopod put out as needed. It becomes anything of roughly its own weight — a chair, a dog, a person — holds the shape indefinitely, and is far more curious about you than hostile.

A cat-sized dragon with scales that shift towards whatever it is sitting on and a barbed sting on its tail. It cannot speak but talks readily enough mind to mind, and it attaches itself to people it likes on terms it sets itself.

A predator with the head and clawed forelimbs of a great cat on the sleek finned body of a seal, roaring loudly enough to carry across open water. It is savagely territorial, very hard to kill, and quite capable of taking a swimmer off a beach.

A furred, richly dressed figure with a beast's head and hands whose palms face backwards — the detail that gives it away to anyone who knows to look. It is vain, cruel and enormously wealthy, sheds hostile magic, and prefers to run a household of victims rather than a fight.

A floating knot of a creature, all mouth and trailing tentacles, with no legs and no need of them. It drifts down on prey from above, holds it with several limbs at once, and its stare leaves a body unable to move while the feeding starts.

A scaled, serpentine thing with a single clawed arm and a long tail, drifting a foot above the ground and radiating a raw, humming vitality. It is not really hostile so much as indiscriminate; what it touches is charged with a life it never asked for.

A vast segmented worm of the far north, limbless, with a fanged maw and plates that glow as its temper rises. It burrows under snow and comes up beneath a camp; the heat off its back is enough to ruin a weapon left touching it.

A bird of prey on an impossible scale, with a wingspan that shades a village square and talons that close around an ox. It nests on the highest crags, sees a moving animal from a great height, and carries off whatever it decides on without pausing.

A tall column of grey rock with one eye and a mouth, indistinguishable from a stalagmite until it opens either. It flicks out long sticky strands, drains the strength out of whatever they touch, and reels the body in unhurried.

A four-legged scavenger the size of a big hound and a good deal heavier than it looks, plated in dull chitin and steering by a pair of long feathery antennae. It smells worked metal across a room and wants nothing else in the world: a touch of those antennae reduces a blade or a breastplate to red flakes, which it then eats.

A huge, scarred boar whose tusks cut like honed steel and take limbs off cleanly. Wounds close on it as fast as they open, ordinary magic slides off, and it charges anything in its territory without any interest in what happens next.

A shark-eyed sea devil, finned and clawed, with a mouth of triangular teeth and a trident in both hands. Sahuagin raid coasts in organised packs, speak with sharks and bring them along, and go berserk at the smell of blood in the water.

A sahuagin born with four arms instead of two, which its people treat as a mark of favour rather than a defect. It fights with a trident and a free hand to spare, and it is usually found leading the ones with the ordinary number.

A sahuagin born looking like a sea elf — slender, fine-featured, with none of the shark about it. Its own people find it repellent and use it anyway: it swims into places no sea devil could approach, and it is entirely loyal to them.

A coiling serpent's body below a humanoid torso, all of it red-hot, carrying a spear it forged itself. Metal near it glows. It wraps and crushes with the tail while the spear does the rest, and it is a better smith than almost anyone it will ever meet.

A goat-legged fey with short horns and a permanent air of having started drinking earlier than you did, carrying pipes, a dagger and a short bow. The pipes are the real weapon; it moves through undergrowth in silence and would rather trick you than fight.

A humanoid torso rising from the body of a great scorpion, with a pincer arm, a raised sting and a pike carried in the free hands. They hold desert country as their own, hate anything that settles in it, and are strong enough to make that stick.

A black hound the size of a mastiff, hard to make out in anything but full daylight, hunting in packs. The baying is the danger: it gets into the nerve and scatters a group, which is precisely what the pack is waiting for.

A heap of rotting creeper and layered vegetation, roughly man-shaped, that reads as a compost pile until it stands up. Fire barely marks it and lightning actively feeds it. It wraps what it catches in vine and squeezes.

A heavy construct built to stand between its owner and harm, bound to an amulet that its owner wears. It takes wounds meant for them, closes its own damage steadily, and follows its instructions with no judgement whatsoever about what they are.

A small blue-grey lizard, harmless-looking and about the length of a forearm, that clings to cave walls in colonies. It senses living things by the charge on them and delivers a shock; several of them together can put a grown adult on the ground.

A rangy, hunched giant with rubbery hide, a foul temper and claws it uses before it thinks. Wounds close while you watch, and severed pieces grow back. Nothing about a troll stops until the wounds are burned or the parts are kept apart.

A troll that lives in water and cannot leave it for long, breathing beneath the surface and hauling victims down from a riverbank or a hull. It regrows what it loses just as readily as its land-bound kin, and it is much harder to burn.

A tall, insubstantial figure of cold shadow, keeping the outline of the person it once was. Blades pass through it. Its touch takes something out of a body that rest does not put back, and sunlight is the one thing it will not face.

A great tawny lion the size of a cart with the maned head and grave face of a man. It is dignified, well-spoken and disinclined to explain itself, sets its own terms for passage, and settles disagreements with claws rather than argument.

A lion's body under the horned head of a ram, heavier and duller than its man-headed cousin and considerably less interested in conversation. It gores with the horns, is greedy about treasure and food alike, and is the one sphinx that will simply charge.

A tawny lion's body carrying the head and face of a woman, watchful and unhurried. She sees through invisibility without effort, trades in riddles and old knowledge, and expects an honest answer in return for one.

A lion's body under the head and hooked beak of a hawk, sharper-eyed than its kin and far stupider. It has no interest in riddles or terms; it bullies what it can, hunts what it cannot bully, and attacks on sight more often than not.

A wasp-bodied hunter the size of a horse with heavy mandibles and a long sting, oily enough that a web cannot hold it. It hunts giant spiders specifically, paralyses one, and lays an egg in it for the larva to eat its way out of later.

A fey the size of a hand, cricket-legged below the waist, carrying a sword and bow scaled to match. It jumps enormous distances, moves in near silence, fiddles beautifully, and takes real delight in leading travellers somewhere they did not mean to go.

A small, green-skinned water fey of ponds and slow rivers, charming in a way that is difficult to argue with. Nixies are solitary and shy of strangers, breathe water, and can grant a guest the same trick for as long as they are welcome.

A tiny winged fey, invisible whenever it prefers to be, carrying a sword and a bow no longer than a finger. It is a relentless prankster, hard to catch and harder to punish, and the arrows are not always meant to be lethal.

A rust-red flying thing the size of a cat, all wings and clutching legs around a long needle proboscis. It fastens on, drives the needle home and drinks until it is full or killed. One is a nuisance; they never come as one.

The largest and worst thing that walks: an armoured horror with fangs, horns, crushing claws and a lashing tail, indifferent to fire and to nearly all magic. Wounds close as fast as they are made. It sleeps for generations and empties a country when it does not.

A shambling heap of vine, root and rotting leaf with a mouth somewhere in the middle of it. It looks like a thicket until it moves. It takes hold with tendrils and swallows, and animals will not go anywhere near where one has been.

A giant of the old order, beautiful and enormous, carrying a mattock built for its own hand and javelins the length of a spar. It is as clever as anything alive, magic mostly fails against it, and its temper is the reason most stories about titans end badly.

A shelled sea creature the size of a large dog, with pincer arms and a hard case pierced by openings it shifts its limbs between. It sees in every direction at once, swims fast, and squirts a blinding ink before it decides whether to fight.

A tree that stands up and walks. Bark-skinned, several times the height of a man and slow to decide anything, it can pass for ordinary timber for as long as it cares to. It strikes with limbs heavy enough to come through a wall, and it fears nothing except fire.

A sea-dweller with silver hair and fine scales, breathing water and moving through it with no effort at all, carrying a trident. Tritons keep to their own deep settlements, mistrust the surface, and defend their waters without much discussion.

A stooped reptilian humanoid with a spiny crest and skin that shifts towards the colour of the rock behind it, armed with stone axe and javelins. The smell is the first thing anyone notices and it is bad enough to make a fighter sick where they stand.

A white horse with a spiral horn, a cloven step and eyes that hold rather more than an animal's. It heals what it touches, cannot be enchanted or poisoned, keeps to one stretch of old forest, and fights anything evil that enters it with the horn first.

The pale, hollow thing left when a vampire feeds without finishing: fanged, cold, casting no reflection, and bound to the will of whatever made it. It climbs sheer walls, closes its own wounds, and cannot cross the thresholds its master's rules forbid.

A severed head the size of a melon with leathery bat wings where the ears should be and a mouth of green teeth, flapping through the dark. Its shriek freezes a victim in place, and its kiss begins turning that victim into another one of it.

A withered corpse with glowing eyes that keeps the bearing and bad temper of whoever it was, and prefers not to leave its own tomb. It knows where the living are without looking, and what its claws take from a person does not come back with rest.

A drifting ball of pale light about the size of a fist, harmless-looking and almost impossible to affect with magic. It leads travellers into bog, cliff and worse, waits for the accident to finish, and it enjoys the whole process.

A wolf grown to the size of a pony, black-furred and cold-eyed, considerably cleverer than any animal has business being. Worgs speak, run in packs, bear riders when it suits them, and eat what they catch while it is still complaining.

A great wolf in frost-white fur, near invisible against snow, with a bite that burns cold and breath that comes out as a killing blast of it. It hunts in packs, talks, and is often found working for whatever larger thing has hired it.

A hooded shape of moving darkness with nothing inside the hood, drifting a little above the floor. Weapons find nothing to bite on. Its touch drains the life out of a body, and what it kills tends to get up and drift after it.

A wraith grown tall and old, colder and considerably cleverer, aware of every living thing in the building around it. It commands lesser wraiths, plans rather than haunts, and drains a life away faster than the smaller kind manage.

A lean red-scaled biped with four arms, fighting with a sword in one pair and a bow in the other. It steps in from another plane, paralyses someone, lays eggs in them and steps back out — the fight is only ever a means to that.

A squat, three-sided creature of living rock with three arms, three legs, three eyes and a mouth on the top of its head. It swims through solid stone the way a fish swims through water, and it wants metal and gems, not people.

A black hound that runs on the air rather than the ground, hunting in packs through the night sky. Its bay is worse than its bite: it empties the nerve of anyone who hears it, and the pack works on whoever breaks first.

A blind flying reptile some twenty feet long, hunting entirely by sound from high above a canyon. It answers with a lance of focused noise that shatters stone, and the only reliable way to hide from it is to be genuinely silent.

A dog-sized beetle in dull brown chitin that smells strongly of something gone wrong. Prodded, it turns its abdomen towards the problem and sprays a jet of boiling caustic fluid, which discourages most things from prodding it twice.

A beetle the length of a forearm with two luminous glands above its eyes that shed a steady red glow for days after it dies. It is barely a threat, and the glands are worth collecting, which is why anyone bothers with them at all.
A heavy black beetle the size of a pony, with enormous branching mandibles it uses on rivals and on anything blocking its way. It is not a hunter, but it will shear through a leg to get past one.

A mantis the size of a horse, green and stick-still among foliage it matches exactly. It waits without moving for as long as it takes, takes prey with two spined forelimbs faster than the eye follows, and eats it while it is held.

An ape built to a scale that makes a bear look reasonable, thickly furred, with arms long enough to reach a rooftop. It climbs anything, throws what it can lift, and its temper is short in a way that leaves very little warning.

A rat the size of a small dog, coarse-furred and quick, at home in sewers, holds and grain stores. It moves almost silently, eats nearly anything, and is bold enough to bite a standing adult when there are enough of them.

A bat with a wingspan wider than a man is tall, furred, with huge ears and small sharp teeth. It hunts on the wing in complete darkness by sound alone, and it is far more alarming to meet in a corridor than it is dangerous.

A flightless bird taller than a man, running on heavy clawed legs behind a deep, hatchet-shaped beak. It is fast over open ground, aggressive out of proportion to its size, and quite willing to run down a mounted traveller.

A lean tan scavenger the size of a small dog, sharp-eared and constantly listening. Jackals follow larger hunters for what is left, run in loose packs, and will take a wounded animal — or a wounded person — that cannot defend itself properly.

A mottled green frog the size of a large dog, sitting motionless in reed shadow with only its eyes above water. Its tongue comes out much further and much faster than anything expects, and it swallows what it catches whole.

The largest and least otherworldly of the genie kinds, made of all four elements at once and living in the world rather than beyond it. Jann keep to deserts, dislike being ordered about by anyone, and fight with a heavy broadsword.

A big, heavy-jawed guard dog, loyal, greedy and famously stubborn once it has decided about someone. It tracks by scent, hears far more than its handler does, and holds what it is told to hold until told otherwise.

A slender winged serpent no longer than an arm, bright-scaled and quick in the air. Its bite burns as well as bleeds, and it can spit the same caustic venom a short distance at anything it would rather not get close to.

A sea-dwelling elf with fine silver-green skin, webbed hands and gills, carrying a short spear and a dagger. Aquatic elves keep to coastal shallows and reefs, live a long time, and grow ill and weak if kept out of the water.
